opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When I think about that move, the biggest shift was going from being deep inside one very specific product problem to looking at the whole stack from the platform side.

At Cruise, everything was organized around one question: can this car drive safely, without a human, on the streets of San Francisco tonight? That focus was incredibly clarifying. You learn very quickly that autonomy isn't one model. It's perception, prediction, planning, simulation, data infrastructure, validation, and operations all tied together. The hard part is usually the long tail, the weird double-parked truck or the construction worker waving you through with a hand signal. You also learn humility. A demo that works 99% of the time is still very far from a product.

What drew me to NVIDIA was the chance to work on that same problem one level up. Instead of solving it for one fleet in one city, the question becomes: what are the foundational tools, models, and compute platforms that let many companies solve it, and not just in driving but in robotics and physical AI more broadly? You stop asking "how do we fix this edge case" and start asking "how do we build systems that make edge cases cheaper to find, simulate, and learn from."

Intellectually, a few things excited me. The first is the convergence I'd been watching. A few years ago autonomous driving was mostly hand-engineered modules. Now large end-to-end models, world models, and generative simulation are actually starting to work, and NVIDIA sits right at the intersection of compute, simulation, and models. The second is scale. When you build infrastructure, your work compounds across a whole ecosystem rather than one vehicle program. The third is that the problem really is broader than cars. A car is essentially a robot with a very constrained action space. The lessons about data flywheels, closed-loop evaluation, and safety carry over to humanoids, manipulation, and industrial robots, and I wanted to be part of that bigger picture.

So it didn't feel like leaving autonomy behind. It felt like taking everything I learned the hard way on the road and asking how to generalize it.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts solving for one fleet with building tools for many companies, but does not say that exploring different companies’ simulation needs is more interesting than pushing simulation to its limit within one company.

r002.rationale: The response mentions simulation and broader autonomy work, but does not identify the simulation requirements of mass-produced L2 autonomous driving as an attraction.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, the biggest shift was going from building one car to building the thing that lets everyone build the car.

At Cruise, the problem was very concrete. You have a fleet, a city, a stack, and every day the question is: what broke last night and how do we fix it so the vehicle is safer tomorrow? That's incredibly satisfying work, because the feedback loop is real. A rider gets in, the car does something awkward at an unprotected left turn, and you can trace that back to a specific model, a specific piece of data, sometimes a specific labeling decision. You learn a lot about what actually matters in the real world versus what looks good on a benchmark.

But after a few years, I started noticing that most of my hardest problems weren't really autonomy problems. They were infrastructure problems. How do you train on petabytes of driving data without the pipeline falling over? How do you run simulation at a scale where you're actually sampling the long tail instead of just replaying the same hundred scenarios? How do you get a model that's great in the data center down onto a compute-constrained box in the trunk without losing the behavior you spent months tuning? Every autonomy team I talked to was rebuilding those same pieces, badly, in parallel.

That's what made NVIDIA interesting. The question stops being "how do we solve San Francisco" and becomes "what's the general shape of this problem, and what's the platform that makes it tractable for everyone?" You get to think one level of abstraction up. And you get to work across the whole stack at once, from silicon all the way to the foundation models, which is just not possible inside a single AV company.

The other thing, and I didn't fully appreciate this until I got there, is that the lessons from driving generalize. Robotics, embodied AI, anything where a model has to act in the physical world under safety constraints, it's all the same family of problems. Perception, world modeling, closed-loop evaluation, sim-to-real. At Cruise I was solving those for one agent in one domain. Now I'm thinking about them as a general capability. That reframing was what pulled me over.

astra-6.text:
For me, the interesting shift was from solving a very specific, demanding problem to thinking about the foundations that enable many different problems to be solved. In autonomous driving, the question is concrete: how do you get a system to perceive the world, make decisions, and behave reliably? That forces you to think across the whole stack.

What appealed to me about NVIDIA was the opportunity to take that systems perspective and apply it more broadly. How do hardware and software need to evolve together? How do you make a capability useful beyond one model or one application? That change in abstraction—from building a particular system to building the platform other people build on—was intellectually exciting.

At Cruise, autonomous driving brought perception, prediction, planning, and real-time computing together in one system. You couldn’t think about a model in isolation; what mattered was how it behaved as part of the whole system.

NVIDIA offered a broader lens on those same questions: how do you design computing platforms and tools that help other teams build intelligent systems? I found that change in perspective intellectually exciting—carrying lessons from a concrete application into more general infrastructure, while still staying close to the constraints of the real world.
